value.overview: The Streaked Flycatcher (Myiodynastes maculatus) is a medium-sized tyrant flycatcher with strongly streaked upperparts and underparts, a broad bill, and a concealed yellow crown patch. It occupies a wide range of tropical habitats from Mexico to southern South America. The species often perches conspicuously in the canopy or on exposed branches, where it watches for flying insects, but it also eats fruit. In Costa Rica, it is associated mainly with the Pacific slope.
value.classification: The Streaked Flycatcher belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers, and the genus Myiodynastes. Several geographic subspecies are recognized; birds in western Costa Rica are generally assigned to the Central American form Myiodynastes maculatus difficilis.
value.identification: This flycatcher is about 20–22 cm long. Adults have a brownish, warm buff or cinnamon back and head marked with heavy dark streaking, a pale throat, and a whitish to yellowish breast and belly covered with prominent dusky streaks. The wings and tail are dark, often with paler edging. A yellow-orange crown patch is usually hidden but may be raised during excitement. Its thick, pale-based bill helps distinguish it from some similar streaked flycatchers.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from Mexico through Central America and much of South America. In Costa Rica it occurs chiefly on the Pacific slope, where it is a resident and also receives migrants from farther north. It uses forest edges, gallery forest, second-growth woodland, plantations, mangroves, open woodland, and pasture or agricultural areas with retained trees. It is most frequent in lowlands and foothills, generally reaching about 1,200 metres in Costa Rica, although local elevation limits can vary.
value.migrationStatus: It is partly migratory. In Costa Rica, the resident Pacific-slope population is supplemented by passage or wintering birds, especially from northern Central America. Some individuals may therefore be present year-round, while numbers and sightings can increase during migration and the nonbreeding season.
value.breeding: Breeding has been recorded in Costa Rica. The species commonly nests in natural cavities, abandoned woodpecker holes, or other enclosed sites in trees, and may sometimes use cavities associated with buildings or structures. The nest is a loose collection of plant material and other debris placed inside the cavity. A clutch usually contains a small number of eggs, commonly two or three. Both adults participate in territory defense and care of the young.
value.dietFeeding: The Streaked Flycatcher feeds mainly on large insects captured from a perch, including beetles, cicadas, grasshoppers, and other flying or exposed arthropods. It may also take small reptiles or other small prey opportunistically. Fruit and berries form an important supplementary part of the diet, particularly when insect prey is less available. It usually hunts from the canopy or an exposed branch, making short sallies to seize prey before returning to the perch.
value.behavior: This species is usually seen singly or in pairs and often sits quietly on a prominent branch while scanning the surroundings. It makes sudden, direct flights to capture insects and may also descend to take fruit. Individuals defend feeding or breeding territories with calls and active displays. During migration, it can occur in loose mixed-species groups, although it is not normally a highly gregarious bird. Its bold posture and conspicuous streaking make it relatively noticeable in open forest habitats.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable.
